kept.title: Mostly instant, now and then a long think
kept.unit: seconds per decision
kept.claim: At Ascension 20 the AI makes a typical move in 0.15 seconds, and three moves in four take under a second. Its slowest move took 96 seconds, though, and the slowest 10% of moves used 73% of all its thinking time.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, all run-rule versions pooled, runs 28-90 (63 runs, 3,579 fight decisions); A0 shown separately, runs 1-27 (27 runs, 1,739 fight decisions)
kept.n: 3,579 A20 decisions; 1,739 A0 decisions
kept.caveat: These are wall-clock seconds on a laptop that other jobs shared, so single times are noisy. A0 and A20 used different net and search versions and different decks, so the two settings aren't a like-for-like comparison. In total the AI thought for about 2.4 hours in the A20 runs and 1.7 hours in the A0 runs. Percentiles take the sorted value at position p*N (linear interpolation gives values up to 0.1 s lower). The slowest-10% share is 72.5%, rounded to 73%.
kept.reason: My own script got the same subsets: 90 runs, A0 = runs 1-27 with 1,739 fight decisions, A20 = runs 28-90 with 3,579 fight decisions. I split decisions.jsonl by floor drops inside each folder and matched each group to that folder's runs that had fights, in runs_of order. 873 card-reward lines were left out, every fight decision has a seconds value, and no decision group was left without a run. The medians match (A20 0.15, A0 0.31). The slowest moves match too: A20 96.14 s against Slime Boss in run 44 on floor 16, and A0 110.66 s against three Red Louses in run 2 on floor 11. Totals match at 2.37 h (A20) and 1.73 h (A0). 74.0% of A20 moves took under a second, so 'three in four' holds. The slowest 10% of A20 moves used 72.4-72.5% of the thinking time, depending on whether 357 or 358 moves count as the top 10%; the miner's 0.73 comes from 358 moves, 72.54%, rounded up. The percentiles differ a little by method. The miner takes the sorted value at index int(p*N) (A20 p90 7.63, p99 28.29); linear interpolation gives 7.54 and 28.20, and A0 gives 12.35 and 28.32. The differences are below 0.1 s and the claim's text doesn't use them. A0 and A20 aren't pooled. Pooling A20 rule versions is fine for thinking time and is labelled. The caveat about noise and A0/A20 not being comparable is correct.

kept.title: Slime Boss is the fight it thinks hardest about
kept.unit: median seconds of thinking per fight
kept.claim: In a typical Slime Boss fight the AI thought for 81 seconds in total. In a typical Hexaghost fight it thought for 2 seconds, and against Gremlin Nob for about 1. Four of the five A20 fights with the most total thinking time were Slime Boss fights, and one of them took 7 minutes 20 seconds.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, all run-rule versions pooled, runs 28-90; median total thinking seconds per fight for selected encounters, each seen at least 14 times (Gremlin Gang pooled over all its gremlin mixes)
kept.n: 582 A20 fights; per row: Slime Boss 20, Gremlin Gang 20, Large Acid Slime 14, Sentries 15, The Guardian 14, Hexaghost 17, Lagavulin 18, Gremlin Nob 21, Jaw Worm 49, Cultist 52
kept.caveat: These are totals for each fight, so longer fights add up more time. The median number of decisions was 12.5 for Slime Boss, 10 for Hexaghost and 13.5 for The Guardian, so fight length alone doesn't explain the gap. The slimes that split off also count toward the Slime Boss fight. The rows are a selection of encounters, not all of them. The fifth fight in the top five was Jaw Worm + Spike Slime (M) at 434 s.
kept.reason: I recomputed every number from all_runs(): 90 runs, runs 28-90 are all A20, 582 A20 fights. All of the boss, elite, Jaw Worm, Cultist and Acid Slime (L) medians match exactly, and so do the n values: Slime Boss 80.9 (n=20, worst 440.4 s), Acid Slime L 23.6 (n=14), Sentries 16.6 (n=15), Guardian 5.4 (n=14), Hexaghost 2.1 (n=17), Lagavulin 1.2 (n=18), Nob 1.1 (n=21), Jaw Worm 0.3 (n=49), Cultist 0.1 (n=52). Four of the five A20 fights with the most total thinking were Slime Boss fights: 440 s (run 44), 343 s, 317 s and 218 s. The other one is Jaw Worm + Spike Slime M in run 49 at 434 s. One row is wrong. The miner grouped fights by their exact set of monster ids, which splits the Gremlin Gang encounter (any 4 random gremlins) into many small groups. The row only covers the 3 fights whose gremlins were exactly {Fat, Thief, Warrior}. Pooling every Gremlin Gang fight (A20, no Nob) gives n=20 with a median of 30.7 s. Two small points: the median number of decisions is 12.5 for Slime Boss and 13.5 for The Guardian (the miner's rounding showed 12 and 14), and the rows are a selection, not every encounter seen at least 3 times.

kept.title: The slowest monsters to think against
kept.unit: mean seconds per decision with the monster alive
kept.claim: With a Sneaky Gremlin on the board, the AI's average move takes 9.5 seconds, and with a large slime (they split when hurt) about 8. Against Gremlin Nob, Cultist or Lagavulin it averages about a second or less, and the typical move takes about 0.15 seconds.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, all run-rule versions pooled, runs 28-90; every fight decision with that monster alive on the board (hp above 0, not escaped); monsters seen in at least 30 decisions across at least 4 runs
kept.n: 3,579 A20 fight decisions in 63 runs; per-row n and run counts in notes
kept.caveat: This is a mean, so a few long thinks pull it up: the slowest 10% of A20 decisions take 73% of all thinking time. Monsters in multi-monster fights bring the other monsters with them. A gremlin is never alone, and much of the slowdown may come from the number of targets (see the board-shape statistic). The Sneaky Gremlin row rests on only 32 decisions. This shows what goes together, not what causes what.
kept.reason: My own script (run split by floor drops, mapped onto real_game_report.all_runs, A20 by the run's ascension, which agrees with view.ascension on all 3,579 decisions; monster alive = hp>0 and not escaped; gen: prefix stripped) reproduces every mean, n and run count, with two exceptions. (1) Gremlin Nob has 103 decisions, not 167. The miner's own stats.py output also says n 103 (runs 21, mean 0.66), so 167 was a copying error. (2) The claim that the typical move takes under a tenth of a second is false: the A20 median is 0.15 s. Under 0.1 s holds only for some monsters (Cultist 0.03, Lagavulin 0.06, Hexaghost 0.07). The word "pushes" also states a cause where the data only shows things that go together, so I reworded it. No A0 data is pooled (1,739 A0 decisions are excluded), there is no double counting, and the gen: prefixes merge correctly (Sneaky, Fat, Mad, Shield gremlins, Gremlin Wizard and the slavers appear only with the prefix).

kept.title: Cards in hand that make it ponder
kept.unit: mean seconds per decision with the card in hand
kept.claim: With Battle Trance in hand the AI averages 7.3 seconds a move, about three times the A20 average. Slimed is the surprise: it is a status card, but you can pay 1 energy to play it, and hands holding it average 6.2 seconds. Dazed and Burn can't be played at all, and hands holding them average under a second.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, all run-rule versions pooled, runs 28-90. Fight decisions with the card in hand (upgraded, plain and cost-modified copies pooled). A selection of the 45 cards seen in at least 30 decisions over at least 4 runs.
kept.n: 3,579 A20 decisions; per row n and runs in notes
kept.caveat: Several cards come from only 5 to 7 runs, so one deck's slow fights can carry the whole row. Fights decide which cards show up: Slimed comes from the slow slime fights, Dazed mostly from Sentries, and Burn from Hexaghost. Read each row as 'moves with this card in hand were slower', not as proof that the card itself slows the search. The A0 list has a different order (True Grit, Wild Strike and Thunderclap at the top), so the ranking isn't stable.
kept.reason:
My own recount gives the same numbers. All 90 runs map cleanly (decisions split per folder where the floor drops), the run-level ascension agrees with view.ascension on every decision, and there are 3,579 A20 fight decisions from runs 28-90 with a mean of 2.385 s. Battle Trance 7.32 (70/5), Slimed 6.21 (312/53), Intimidate 5.92 (42/7), Inflame 5.17 (32/6), Anger 4.73 (294/16), Pommel Strike 3.96 (178/17), Havoc 1.10 (103/5), Burn 0.82 (75/19) and Dazed 0.67 (139) all match. 7.32/2.39 = 3.06, so "about three times" holds. Slimed costs 1, and Burn and Dazed are unplayable, so that wording is right.

Fixes needed:
(1) The caveat says Dazed comes from Sentries and Hexaghost. That is wrong. Hexaghost gives Burn (71 of 75 Burn decisions are against Hexaghost). Dazed comes mostly from Sentries (114 of 139), plus a few from The Guardian.
(2) The Dazed note says "19+ runs". It is exactly 21 runs.
(3) Reckless Charge is 7.175 s, so rounding gives 7.17 or 7.18. Small detail; 7.2 is safest.
(4) The miner's name cleaner strips "gen:" and "+" but not suffixes like "{cost=0/combat}", so a few copies with a changed cost are counted as separate cards. Strike gets n=3,063, not 3,060, with the mean unchanged at 2.14. Defend and Bash shift by 1 each.
(5) The rows are a selection from 45 qualifying A20 cards. The subset text should say so. One left out: Metallicize (0.90 s, 30 decisions, 8 runs) is a playable card that is also under a second.

No pooling of A0 and A20, no double counting, and no problems from the "gen:" prefix or from upgrades.

kept.title: When the search runs out of room
kept.unit: % of decisions that hit the node cap
kept.claim: The search stops when it reaches a fixed number of positions (its node cap). At A20 that happened on 9% of moves, and the rate varies a lot with what is in play. With Evolve active it hit the cap on 57% of moves, with Juggernaut 51% (both largely from a single run), and on 43% of the moves where it drank a potion. With Dexterity active it almost never did (1%).
kept.subset: Real game, A20, all run-rule versions pooled, runs 28-90; share of fight decisions where the search hit its node cap (cut = true). A0 runs 1-27 shown separately for comparison.
kept.n: 3,579 A20 decisions, 313 hit the cap; A0 runs 1-27: 241 of 1,739

rows.label: Evolve active
rows.note: 58 decisions, 4 runs; run 89 alone 21 of 27, others 12 of 31 (39%)

rows.label: Juggernaut active
rows.note: 89 decisions, 4 runs; run 89 alone 22 of 30, others 23 of 59 (39%)

kept.caveat: Evolve and Juggernaut each come from only 4 runs, and one run (89, which had both) gives about half of their decisions and most of their capped ones. Without it both rates are about 39%, and one Juggernaut run never hit the cap. A potion adds its own targets to the options, and the AI tends to drink one in hard spots, so the 43% is about the spot as much as the potion. These are associations, not causes, and a capped move isn't necessarily a worse move.
kept.reason: My own script reproduces every number. I split decisions.jsonl into runs where the floor drops, matched each run to runs_of() and got 90 runs with no decision left unmatched. A20 (runs 28-90): 313 of 3,579 capped (8.7%). A0 (runs 1-27): 241 of 1,739 (13.9%). Evolve 33/58, Juggernaut 45/89, potion move 39/91 (mean 9.7 s), Battle Trance in hand 28/70, Spike Slime (L) alive 54/158, Frail 61/319, Dexterity 1/139, Burn 0/75. Run counts and the subset are right, and A0 and A20 are not pooled. Pooling the A20 rule versions is allowed here because the cut field is fight-level behaviour. One small difference: I count 1,734 Strike moves (Strike and Strike+), or 1,722 for plain Strike only, against the miner's 1,733; the rate is 5.0% either way. The real problem is concentration. Run 89 alone gives 21 of the 33 capped Evolve moves (21/27) and 22 of the 45 capped Juggernaut moves (22/30). Without run 89 both rates fall to about 39% (Evolve 12/31, Juggernaut 23/59). Juggernaut run 62 never hit the cap (0/11), and neither did Evolve run 73 (0/8). So the 57% and 51% are mostly one run's fights. The caveat must say so, and the claim should not say the rate "depends" on cards (that is causal wording).

kept.title: How often it skips the whole card reward
kept.unit: % of card rewards skipped
kept.claim: About one card reward in five, the AI takes nothing: it rates 'skip' above every card offered. At Ascension 0 it got pickier late in the act (about a third skipped on floors 13-17); at Ascension 20 the skip rate barely moves with the floor.
kept.subset: Real game, card-reward screens. A0: runs 1-27 (run rules 1). A20: runs 28-90, all run-rule versions and fight-guard settings pooled (picks are run-level, so treat the pooled A20 row as a mix of settings).
kept.n: A0: 319 rewards in 27 runs; A20: 554 rewards in 63 runs
kept.caveat: The AI always took the option it scored highest (873 of 873 rewards), so a skip means the net scored the deck without the card higher. A0 floors 18+ come from the 16 of 27 A0 runs that reached Act 2, with only 45 rewards in all; no A20 run got past floor 17. By setting within A20, the skip rate ranges from 10% to 33%, but the groups with the extreme rates are tiny (10-21 rewards each). The two large groups, rules 2 (148 rewards) and rules 5 with the fight guard (298 rewards), sit at 16% and 18%, so treat the spread as noise.
kept.reason: My own script reproduces every number exactly. It uses all_runs() for the 90 runs and settings, and splits decisions.jsonl into runs where the floor drops: each folder's number of runs matches. A0 has 62 of 319 skips in 27 runs, by floor band 20/128, 13/86, 19/60 and 10/45. A20 has 100 of 554 in 63 runs, by band 46/274, 33/174 and 21/106. The pick was the top-scored option in 873 of 873 rewards. A0 and A20 are kept apart. Runs 3 and 5 add only 2 rewards each and run 21 adds 11, so they barely affect the totals. Because I matched the miner's numbers, I did not need to read the miner's script. Three wording problems need fixing. (1) 'Above all three cards': 9 rewards offered 4 cards, so say 'above every card offered'. (2) The caveat says A0 floors 18+ come from 'the few runs that reached Act 2', but 16 of the 27 A0 runs have rewards on floor 18 or later, which is not few. (3) 'Most of those groups have 10-21 rewards' is wrong. The A20 setting groups have 56, 148, 21, 21, 10 and 298 rewards, and only three of the six are that small. The A0 rise on floors 13-17 (19/60 against about 15% earlier) is a description, not a stated cause, so it may stand.

kept.title: A20: how much the net likes a card over skipping
kept.unit: score points above the skip option (mean per offer)
kept.claim: Averaged over every offer, the net scores adding Rampage or Fire Breathing about a third of a point above skipping. Fire Breathing was the pick in 3 of the 5 most one-sided rewards and in 5 of the 7 most one-sided. Berserk, Entrench, Limit Break and Feel No Pain score below an empty pick on average: the scorer rates the deck lower with them than without them.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, runs 28-90, all run-rule versions pooled (card picks are run-level; rules 1-5 and fight guard 0/1 mixed). For each offer: the card's score minus the skip option's score, averaged per card; upgraded offers counted with their card (one Barricade+ offer). Cards offered at least 8 times. "Most one-sided" = largest gap between the best and second-best option in a reward.
kept.n: 554 card rewards (all with a skip option); per-card offer counts in notes
kept.caveat: The scores are the reward scorer's own numbers (most options score about 1.4-3), not win chances, and they depend on the deck at the time. The margins between cards are small (most are within ±0.15), and a single 8-22 offer mean can shift a lot because of one lopsided reward. Cards near the cutoff (Berserk with 8, Bludgeon with 9, Rampage with 10) rest on very few offers. A card can have a high average margin but a middling pick rate when it often shows up next to something the net likes even more (Demon Form: +0.29, picked 4 of 11). Run-rule versions 1-5 are pooled, so the decks at offer time differ between versions.
kept.reason: I recomputed every per-card mean margin and offer count independently and they match: 554 A20 card rewards in runs 28-90, every reward has a skip option, and none from Ascension 0 (319) are mixed in. Barricade gives -0.056 over 14 offers only when one upgraded "Barricade+" offer (run 80) is counted with it. Without it I get -0.057 over 13. That is a defensible merge but should be stated. There are two real errors. (1) The sentence "Fire Breathing was the clear pick in 4 of the 5 most one-sided rewards" is false. Ranking rewards by best score minus second-best (the miner's extra.py) or by best minus skip, the top 5 picks are Fire Breathing (run 59), Fire Breathing (47), Rampage (88), Fire Breathing (60) and Demon Form (34). Fire Breathing was picked in 3 of the 5. It was offered in 4 of them, but in run 88 it sat next to the Rampage that was picked, scoring only 0.08 above skip. Of the 7 most one-sided rewards, it was picked in 5. (2) The bottom of the table leaves out Berserk: 8 offers meets the stated cutoff of at least 8, and its -0.118 is the lowest of any card. Smaller point: "the net expects the deck to do better without them" puts a belief in the net's mouth. All the data shows is that the scorer gives a lower score to the deck with the card than to the deck without it.

kept.title: It doesn't chase rares
kept.unit: % of offered cards picked
kept.claim: Rare cards don't excite it: at Ascension 20 it took 29% of the rares it could pick, against 27% of commons and 27% of uncommons. At Ascension 0, uncommons were its favourite rarity (31%), and rares were no more popular than commons (26% against 25%).
kept.subset: Real game, Ironclad card rewards from floor 1 on (Neow's floor-0 colorless choice left out). Counts only the cards the bot could take: 28 offered cards the engine doesn't model, such as Battle Trance and Reaper, are left out. Rarity comes from the game's own card data in states.jsonl. A0: runs 1-27 (run rules 1). A20: runs 28-90, all run-rule versions and both fight-guard settings pooled.
kept.n: A0: 929 pickable cards in 314 rewards; A20: 1,641 pickable cards in 548 rewards
kept.caveat: It can take at most one card per reward, so these rates are capped by its skip rate (about 18-20%) and by the other cards in the same reward. Rare samples are small (91 and 152 cards), and a few points' difference is within noise. The A0 uncommon lead is about 2 standard errors. Cards the engine doesn't model were never pickable and are left out. Counting them as offered would put A0 rares at 24% (24 of 100) and A0 uncommons at 30%. The A20 figures pool run-rule versions 1-5.
kept.reason: My own script (run numbering and settings from real_game_report.all_runs, decisions split per folder by floor drops and matched to runs; 90 runs, 27 at A0 and 63 at A20, 319 and 554 rewards, no mismatches) reproduces the miner's rows exactly, but only when "offered" means the engine's pickable options. Counting the game's card_reward lists instead gives 966 cards at A0 and 1,662 at A20. The gap is 28 cards the engine doesn't model (Battle Trance, Reaper, Juggernaut, Dual Wield and others), all uncommon or rare. Those cards never appear in options, so the bot could not take them. Counting them as offered drops A0 rares to 24% (24/100) and A0 uncommons to 30%. So the subset has to say "cards it could take", not "cards offered". There is a second issue: the floor-0 rewards (6 at A20, 5 at A0) are Neow's colorless cards (Trip, Swift Strike, Panacea...). They are pooled into common/uncommon even though they are not Ironclad rewards, so I dropped them. Without them: A0 uncommon 31% (96/307), A20 common 27% (245/896), uncommon 27% (160/593), rare unchanged. The conclusions hold. The A20 rates are flat, and A0 rares (26%) are close to commons (25%). The A0 uncommon lead (about 6 points) is modest, about 2 standard errors. Other checks: no gen: splits (names are compared after stripping gen: and +), and no Ascension 0/20 pooling. Pooling run-rule versions is disclosed, but this is a run-level stat, so the label needs to say "all run-rule versions pooled" (it does). Skip rate is 19-20% at A0 and 18% at A20.

There are 4,812 heuristic rewards and 4,958 product rewards. Of the 31 cards offered at least 30 times to each player, Demon Form has by far the biggest gap: 162/238 = 68.1% for the hand-written player against 49/250 = 19.6% for the net, a 48.5-point gap. The game's own state confirms the Shield Gremlin was alive with 0 Block during the standoff.

Note on wording: the Mad Gremlin had 11 Block at the start of every standoff turn from turn 5 on (7 on turn 4). The 75 count comes from the game's state log, because decisions.jsonl records only the first decision of each turn.

kept.title: The longest fights: an 84-turn gremlin standoff
kept.unit: turns
kept.claim: The longest real-game fight lasted 84 turns. In A20 run 83 (floor 5), a Shield Gremlin with 4 HP shielded the remaining Mad Gremlin, giving it 11 Block every turn, for about 69 turns (turns 14 to 82). On 67 of those turns the net struck the shielded Mad Gremlin rather than the 4-HP Shield Gremlin. The two strikes scored almost the same (1.51 vs 1.49). Its HP drained from 35 to 15 before it finally killed the Shield Gremlin, and it won on 8 HP. The A0 record has a different cause. In run 18, floor 2, a Small Acid Slime sat at 4 HP for about 23 turns while the net played Defend, Defend, End. Every option scored exactly the same (2.01), so to the search killing the slime looked no better than waiting.

The two long stalls come from the search seeing no difference between options (A0: every option scored 2.01) or almost none (A20 run 83: 1.51 vs 1.49), not from the monsters. A20 has 582 fights in runs 28-90 and A0 has 272 in runs 1-27. The median is 4 turns at both ascensions. Every listed row matches: turns, won/lost, HP and monster names. In states.jsonl the A20 run 52 Slaver is SlaverBlue, so 'Blue Slaver' is right. Run 83 F5 checks out. The Shield Gremlin sat at 4 HP from turn 3 until it died on turn 82. The surviving Mad Gremlin (21 HP) had 11 Block every turn from turn 14. Player HP was 35 from turn 13, 25 at turn 70, 15 by turn 79, and 8 at the win on turn 84. At turn 14 the scores were Strike on the Mad Gremlin 1.51 and Strike on the Shield Gremlin 1.489. Run 18 F2 also checks out. The Acid Slime (S) was at 4 HP from turn 4 to turn 28, HP stayed 79, the picks over turns 4-28 were Defend 23 times and Strike twice, and every option scored 2.01 on 24 of those decisions. Four fixes are needed. (1) 'Each turn the net struck the shielded Mad Gremlin' is too strong: on turns 14-82 it struck that gremlin on 67 turns and played Defend, End or the Shield Gremlin strike once each. (2) 'the top of the value scale' is not supported: real-game two-turn scores reach 2.14, so 2.01 is not the top. Say only that all options scored the same (2.01). (3) The A20 list leaves out a tie: run 52 F5 (Fat Gremlin x2, Sneaky Gremlin, Gremlin Wizard) also lasted 15 turns, won, HP 79 to 22, the same length as run 28's listed Guardian fight. (4) Run 56 F14 is a smaller stall of the same kind: the Blue Slaver sat at 6 HP from turn 7 to turn 18 while HP fell from 23 to 5. Optional to mention. Run splitting and the A0/A20 separation are correct. Pooling A20 rule versions is acceptable because fight length is fight-level behaviour, and the subset says so.

rows.note: Defend the sole one-turn favourite in 47

My own script reproduces the headline numbers. I read decisions.jsonl directly and split by view.ascension, then kept uncut decisions with at least two options. A20: 3,175 decisions, 630 picks outside the one-turn best set (19.8%), median one-turn cost 0.64 HP-equivalents (score x100), 71 above 5. A0: I get 1,448 decisions and 308 changes (21.3%) against the miner's 1,446 and 307. The miner joins decisions to fights.jsonl rows, so a decision without a fight row drops out. That difference is negligible.

The swap rows are distorted by ties. In 343 of the 630 A20 changes, two or more options tie for the best one-turn score. The miner names the 'from' card as the first tied option in list order, and the list order is Strike, Defend, Bash, and so on. Two rows follow from that order alone. 'Strike -> Bash+' (12) is 12 of 12 tie cases, and 'Strike -> Bash' (11) is 10 of 11. In those cases Bash was also tied for best at one turn, so the change only switched which enemy Bash hit. Ties also undercount cards that come later in the list. Bash was a one-turn favourite overruled for Strike 37 times, not 16. Potions are split by potion name and left out of the rows; slot-0 potion to Strike happened 28 times.

The headline comparison holds when a swap counts any one-turn favourite: Defend to Strike 138, Strike to Defend 24, both matching the miner exactly. Of the 138, Defend was the only one-turn favourite in 47 and tied with another option in 91. The claim's wording 'the one that scores best' should allow ties. A0 and A20 stay separate, and pooling the rule versions is fine for a fight-level stat.

kept.title: Cards the net most wants to play rather than end the turn
kept.unit: median score gain over ending the turn, x100 (roughly HP)
kept.claim: At A20, when Rampage or Ghostly Armor was playable, the net typically scored playing it about 22 points above ending the turn right there. Havoc came last at about 6. Havoc plays the top card of your draw pile and exhausts it, and the net gave it the smallest edge over ending the turn. Its decisions come from only 5 runs.
kept.subset: Real game, A20, runs 28-90, all run-rule versions pooled. 3,266 uncut decisions where End was an option. Per card or potion: the best two-turn score among options that start by playing it (the same card aimed at several targets counts once), minus End's two-turn score in the same decision. Only cards and potions with at least 20 such decisions.
kept.n: 57 cards and potions with n >= 20, each shown with its n (decisions); the number of runs behind each is in the notes
kept.caveat: This measures each card in the hands where it showed up, not the card on its own. Ending a turn with unused energy is always costly, and a card held during desperate fights picks up that context. Many cards come from only a handful of runs (Havoc and Ghostly Armor from 5 each), so their values reflect a few decks. Turns close to lethal pull the averages far up, so medians are shown. At A0 (runs 1-27, 1,498 decisions) the top cards were Defend+ (+18.5, n=77) and Searing Blow (+17.9, n=20, 2 runs), and the bottom card was Demon Form (+3.5, n=28, 3 runs).
kept.reason:
My own script reproduces almost every row exactly: Rampage 22.5 (n=27), Ghostly Armor 22.3 (63), Perfected Strike+ 21.6 (25), Flex 19.7 (84), Shockwave 19.1 (35), Speed Potion 17.7 (22), Carnage 17.5 (61), Fire Breathing 12.0 (70), Intimidate 11.2 (32), Whirlwind 10.1 (36) and Havoc 6.4 (96). It also gets 3,266 A20 decisions and 57 entries with n >= 20. "Uncut" is right: every cut decision has two = null, so the miner's filter on two = null is the same thing.

Three things need fixing.
(1) Spot Weakness is wrong. The miner skips options whose action list is longer than one, but those lists are the same card aimed at several targets, grouped because they reach the same state ("Spot Weakness@0","Spot Weakness@1"). Spot Weakness is the card most often grouped this way. Counting those 8 decisions gives 17.9 with n=81, not 17.7 with n=73. Body Slam is affected the same way but has too few decisions to be listed.
(2) The A0 figure in the caveat should be 1,498 decisions, not 1,496. The miner dropped 2 decisions whose floor had no fight record. The A0 card values are unchanged.
(3) Havoc's description is wrong. Havoc plays the top card of your draw pile and exhausts it; it does not pick a random card. The idea that the net sees this as a gamble it values lowest is a guess. Also, Havoc's 96 decisions come from only 5 runs, and Ghostly Armor's 63 come from only 5 runs, so they reflect a few decks, not a general habit.
A0 and A20 are kept apart (checked with view.ascension: A20 Strike and Defend appear in 63 runs, A0 in 27). Pooling run-rule versions is allowed here because this is fight-level behaviour. No "gen:" duplicates remain.

kept.title: Powers look better two turns deep
kept.unit: % of decisions where looking two turns ahead raised the card's value over ending the turn
kept.claim: How much more a card is worth with two turns of lookahead. For most cards, looking two turns ahead raises the card's value over ending the turn in about 6 decisions of 10 (Strike 57-62%, Defend 62-65%). Some stand out. At A0, Demon Form rose in 25 of 28 decisions. At A20, Bash rose in 362 of 510 (71%), but Bash+ rose in only 59%, so the reason isn't clear. At the other end, an A20 Weak Potion rose in only 10 of 29 decisions, and at A0 Slimed rose in 23 of 61.
kept.subset: Real game, uncut decisions where End was an option. A0: runs 1-27, 1,498 decisions. A20: runs 28-90, all run-rule versions pooled, 3,266 decisions. Per decision and card, the card's option with the best two-turn score counts. Value = share of those decisions where its two-turn gain over End > its one-turn gain over End.
kept.n: per row as noted; cards with at least 20 decisions (Strike/Defend shown as the baseline)
kept.caveat: The one-turn and two-turn scores come from the same net searched to different depths. Two-turn gains over End run larger for almost every card, so compare each row with the Strike/Defend baseline, not with 50%. A rise means the deeper search found more value, not that the card is better in the game. Rows near 25-30 decisions carry about +/-17 points of noise. A20 Inflame, Evolve and Shockwave are not distinguishable from the baseline.
kept.reason:
Every row reproduces exactly with my own script, using the miner's definition. Per decision and card, I took the card's option with the best two-turn score and checked whether its two-turn gain over End beat its one-turn gain over End, with potions named from view.player.potions. Uncut decisions with End: A20 = 3,266 (matches). A0 = 1,498, not 1,496: the miner reaches decisions through fights.jsonl by floor, which drops 2. The rows are unchanged by this.

The wording misleads in three ways:
1. It leaves out the baseline. Ordinary cards also rise most of the time: Strike 57% at A0 and 62% at A20, Defend 62% and 65%. Two-turn gains over End are simply larger in general. A20 Evolve (67%) sits at the Defend baseline. Inflame at 20 of 27 and Shockwave at 26 of 35 are within noise of it (about +/-17 points at n of about 27).
2. The 'powers' story is cherry-picked. A20 Demon Form rose in only 6 of 12. Fire Breathing and Rage are no higher than the baseline. Bash and Shockwave are not powers.
3. The causal reason given for Bash is not supported. Bash+ also applies Vulnerable, and for longer, yet rose in only 294 of 502 (58.6%) at A20, below Strike and Defend.

What holds up: A0 Demon Form at 25 of 28 is far above the roughly 60% baseline. A20 Bash at 362 of 510 is clearly above it. A20 Weak Potion (10 of 29), A0 Slimed (23 of 61) and A0 Blood for Blood (11 of 30) are clearly below it.

No pooling problems. Ascension 0 and 20 are split. Pooling the A20 run-rule versions is acceptable for a fight-level stat. Runs map correctly, 90 in all, and the gen: prefix is stripped.
